articles.title: Walk In Humility
articles.subtitle: By Rev. Dr. Eu Hong Seng, Chairman, NECF
articles.content:
“The reward for humility and fear of the Lord is riches and honor and life.” Proverbs 22:4

In 2025, the theme for our 40-Day Fast and Prayer was “Walking in the Fear of the Lord”. A fitting follow-up for 2026 is “Walk in Humility”.

Humility is so foundational in our walk. It is so vital that the LORD, through the prophet Micah makes His expectations unmistakably clear – “He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” Micah 6:8 (NKJV)

The judgment pronounced against the arrogant in the Day of the LORD serves as a sober admonition to urgently cultivate humility and complete dependence on God. Malachi 4:1 (NKJV) warns us, “For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven, and all the proud, yes, all who do wickedly will be stubble. And the day which is coming shall burn them up,” says the Lord of hosts.

Scripture consistently underscores that pride is never rewarded. The Bible repeatedly teaches that pride comes before the fall and that the Lord Himself opposes and humbles the proud (see Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 29:23; James 4:6).

In contrast, humility comes before honour (see Proverbs 18:12). True submission to the Lord is impossible without humility, and it is those who walk humbly that He exalts.

Scripture repeatedly highlights the blessings and glory that flow from a humble posture:

For the Lord takes pleasure in His people; He will beautify the humble with salvation (Psalm 149:4 NKJV).

Likewise you younger people, submit yourselves to your elders. Yes, all of you be submissive to one another, and be clothed with humility, for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5 NKJV)

Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up. (James 4:10 NKJV).

Our lack of humility often reveals itself in subtle but telling ways. One such expression can be seen during leadership transitions, when churches or ministries are quickly renamed to reflect a new leader’s identity. Yet this was not Isaac’s response.

In Genesis 26:18 we read, “Isaac dug again the wells of water which they had dug in the days of Abraham his father, for the Philistines had stopped them up after the death of Abraham. He called them by the names which his father had called them.”

Isaac restored the old wells of Abraham and retained the names his father had given them. He did not rename them nor rebrand them. He chose honour over self-promotion and personal recognition. In contrast, modern ministry culture can sometimes reflect a subtle desire for personal legacy rather than honouring the faithful labour of those who built the work before us.

Genuine humility is what the Lord seeks. We are cautioned against “fake humility” in Colossians 2:18 (NKJV) which says, “Let no one cheat you of your reward, taking delight in false humility…”

What makes pride especially corrosive is that it resists correction. Money can tempt, anger can flare, and desire can fade – but pride digs in. It hardens opinions into dogma, turns disagreement into offence, and transforms healthy self-respect into self-worship.

Where pride isolates, humility connects. Where pride insists, humility listens. Where pride blinds, humility lets light in.

If money is accused of corrupting what we value, pride corrupts how we see – truth, ourselves and others.

The love of money is indeed the root of all evil. Perhaps a close companion is pride. Pride manifests in many forms, including arrogance, haughtiness, stubbornness, overconfidence, conceit, boastfulness, condescension, and self-promotion.

False humility is a deceptive display – appearing modest while masking pride. It is often driven by a desire for approval and recognition. Genuine humility, however, is marked by dependence on God and a servant-hearted posture toward others. False humility is self-centred and self-serving; true humility seeks the glory of God and the good of others.

As believers, we are called to reject hypocrisy and walk in sincere humility. May we never forget that our Lord Jesus lived His life in lowliness and humility.

Let us bow our heads and hearts in reverence – there is no other way to be humble before our God.

articles.title: Humility Is Foundational to Revival
articles.subtitle: By Rev. Andy Chi, Secretary General
articles.content:
In 2 Chronicles 7:14, the Lord says:

…“if My people, who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.”

Having completed the temple, Solomon offered a prayer of dedication, asking the Lord to hear His people whenever they prayed in or toward the temple. He cried out for God to respond with mercy and intervention when they faced calamities, wars, and even exile because of their sins.

God’s answer to Solomon revealed clear conditions for His intervention—conditions that can be summed up in three words: humility, hunger, and holiness. When His people seek Him with humble hearts, a deep hunger for His presence, and lives set apart for Him, He promises to hear their prayers, forgive their sins, and bring healing and revival to their land.

One of the goals of the 40-Day Fast and Prayer initiative is to spark revival in both the Church and the nation. With millions still waiting to hear the gospel and with the Church in many places losing her way, our need for revival has never been greater. That is why the theme “Walk in Humility” is so timely. True revival always begins when God’s people first humble themselves before Him.

Jesus Himself gives us the perfect example of what it means to walk in humility. From the cradle to the cross, He lived in complete obedience to the Father’s will. This humility was not a weakness. Instead, His life was marked by strength, courage, and unwavering faith—even in suffering, rejection, and death—to fulfil God’s eternal purpose. His devotion to God did not make Him proud or distant; instead, in humility, He served sinners, welcomed children, and even washed His disciples’ feet.

The result of His humble walk was a powerful move of God in Israel, the restoration of the truth of God’s Word, and the unfolding of God’s great plan of salvation for all humanity.

As we begin this new season of prayer and fasting, let us take time to search our hearts and humble ourselves before the Lord. Let us come to Him with prayers of repentance, reverence, and full surrender to His will. May we be found humble in His sight, and may our prayers rise before Him for the revival of the Church and the healing of our land.

articles.title: Humble Yourself under the Mighty Hand of God
articles.subtitle: By Pastor Samuel Ang, Former Secretary-General
articles.content:
Proverbs 22:4, Micah 6:8 (NKJV)

The reward for humility and fear of the Lord is riches, and honour and life

Micah 6:8 (NKJV)

He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God?

This year’s theme “Walk in Humility” will be very challenging for most of us. It is easy to verbalise, but being truly humble requires action through appropriate discipline and commitment. When a person has been recognised as humble, it reflects his fear of the Lord. That was exactly how the Bible describes Moses in Numbers 12:3 - as"very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth,"- leading to blessings of wealth, respect, and a long life.

It also signifies that his strength was under control with a deep submission to God's will, even despite his powerful leadership and occasional displays of anger. His meekness was evident in his handling of conflict, his willingness to intercede for his people, and his humble recognition of God's ultimate power, even when he was challenged.

What did Moses learn from God about humility?

God did not immediately intervene when Moses faced trouble for trying to help his fellow men as a prince of Egypt. He had assumed his people would recognise that God was working through him to rescue them. Taking matters into his own hands and acting rashly, he eventually became afraid and ran, becoming a fugitive as a result. Even as Moses tried to be faithful to fulfill his calling, God used these difficult circumstances to train him in humility. Finally, Moses reached a turning point where he chose God over the power of Egypt.

After 40 years of leading Egypt’s great armies, Moses was then humbled, reduced to leading fragile sheep for the next 40. Instead of addressing thousands of people as a powerful orator, he learned to talk to animals. Moses never intended to become a shepherd after leaving Egypt, but as the years passed, his illusions of grandeur began to fade. He gradually had to align his destiny with God’s will.

Moses found peace living as a humble shepherd for his father-in-law, Jethro (Exodus 2:21). He learned to lead sheep, unaware that God would later call him to lead people. Most importantly, Moses realised that all his knowledge and abilities couldn’t bring him wealth and true greatness - only God could. (Zechariah 4:6).

Moses was not a weak man, even though his meekness was mentioned by none other than God Himself. His meekness was strength under God’s control - a quality that enabled him to lead over a million people out of Egypt into the Promised Land. His meekness helped him to patiently navigate harsh remarks from Pharaoh. Instead of seeing himself as important, he knew he was inadequate and needed God. This transformation from the Moses who had left Egypt happened because he yielded his humble life to God’s purpose.

Let us remember the following objectives:

Just like Moses, God has a calling and a plan for each of us. Even when we make mistakes, doubt His calling or try to limit Him, we must remember that He will never leave us nor forsake us.

When we let humility transform us, both individually and collectively, God can do much more powerful things through us than we could ever imagine. We must follow Moses’ example and stay kind and caring, even when faced with people who are stiff-necked and disobedient.

Finally, remember that God saved Moses as an infant. Moses eventually saw that when God is involved, everything works together for good. Unlike the Pharaoh who asked, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey?”, we should choose to follow and obey God. When we do, our outlook will change completely, and we will be ready to serve Him at any stage in life - even at the age of 80.

Because of Moses’ humility, God was able to use him in extraordinary ways. He wrote the first five books of the Bible. He became God’s prophet who foreshadowed Christ. He was even present with Christ and Elijah during the transfiguration. Most importantly, Moses spoke with God face to face as a friend. That alone is the greatest honour any Christian could desire.

articles.title: Support NECF’s Building Fund
articles.subtitle: By Elder Lee Choong San, Honorary Treasurer, NECF
articles.content:
In 1 Chronicles 29, King David proclaimed to the people of Israel that God had chosen his son Solomon, despite his youth and inexperience, to build the temple. In the same breath, David acknowledged that the work was great and, more importantly, that it was not for man but for the Lord God.

In his deep devotion to the house of God, David then committed incredible amounts of his personal resources to the building of the temple. His example inspired the leaders, captains and officers of Israel and they followed suit, giving freely and willingly for the temple’s construction.

David blessed the Lord before all the assembly and proclaimed in 1 Chronicles 29:13-15:

“And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name. But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.”

This year’s theme, “Walk in Humility”, reminds us of the importance of staying humble in God’s mighty presence. David’s words on behalf of himself and his people, is an acknowledgement that, when we give, it is not about ourselves but all about God. We give not to bring attention to ourselves but to glorify His name (v13).

When we give out of our resources to support the work of God, we are merely acting as stewards of God’s resources and giving back to Him what has always been His. We are often reminded that we journey through life on earth as aliens and pilgrims, and that our time on earth is not permanent but a shadow that will disappear. Let us not hold on to the riches we have been blessed with, but let us bless the Lord with our devotion for the work of His kingdom on earth.

Please continue to sow generously into the kingdom of God this year. Your offerings will be channelled to the NECF Building Fund for the ongoing construction of Wisma NECF, a training and resource centre in Cyberjaya, Selangor.

The construction of the building is progressing smoothly and your generous contributions will ensure its timely completion. This space will serve many Christians for generations to come and stand as a powerful testimony of God’s goodness in our lives. Once completed, you can humbly declare before God as David did - “But who am I, that I am able to offer so willingly as this?”

In closing, we remember David as a man after God’s own heart, who will do all His will. Nothing exemplifies this more than David’s very own words in 1 Chronicles 29:3 – “Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God.”

May God give you the heart of David and bless you abundantly for all that you give.

Thank you.

articles.title: The Posture God Requires
articles.subtitle: Day 1: Friday, 7 August 2026
articles.content:
Micah 6:8

“He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?”

As we begin these 40 days of fasting and prayer, the Lord is calling us back to the foundation of true devotion—a humble walk with Him. Humility is not about how we look; it is an inward posture of the heart that recognises our total dependence on God for life, wisdom, and direction.

Fasting has a way of revealing what lies beneath the surface. As our physical strength decreases, our spiritual condition becomes clearer. To walk humbly with God means allowing God to search us, correct us, and realign our hearts with His will. It is choosing surrender over self-reliance, repentance over defensiveness, and obedience over comfort.

Micah spoke to a people who were faithful in religious practices but distant in their hearts. God reminded them that He was not seeking impressive sacrifices, but lives shaped by humility, justice, and mercy. In the same way, our fasting is not meant to impress God, but to position ourselves before Him — open, teachable, and responsive.

Humility draws us closer to God. It softens our hearts toward others and sharpens our sensitivity to His voice. As we humble ourselves, God promises grace, renewal, and guidance. Let these 40 days be a sacred journey of slowing down, listening deeply, and walking closely with our God.

One Practical Step

Begin each day of the fast with a prayer of surrender:

“Lord, I humble myself before You today. Search my heart, lead my steps, and teach me to walk in Your ways.”
prayers: Lord, reveal areas of pride and self-reliance in my life. Teach me to walk humbly, obediently, and closely with You.
Lord, unite Your people in humility. Remove pride, division, and complacency. Shape us into a people who reflect Your justice and mercy.
Lord, we humble ourselves on behalf of our nation. Heal our land, restore righteousness, and turn hearts back to You.

articles.title: Guarding the Heart from Pride
articles.subtitle: Day 2: Saturday, 8 August 2026
articles.content:
Preparing Our Hearts for 40 Days of Fasting & Prayer

Deuteronomy 17:19–20

“and he shall read it all the days of his life...that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers…”

Let us prepare our hearts today for our daily fasting as the Lord draws our attention to a quiet but powerful warning in Deuteronomy 17:19–20. God commanded Israel's future kings to read His Word daily — not to gain authority, but to guard his heart. Did the kings do that? We must never let our leadership, position, knowledge, or spiritual maturity lead to pride. Verse 20 reminds us that the greatest danger is not just disobedience alone, but having a heart “lifted up” in arrogance above others.

God’s Word keeps us grounded. Daily engagement with Scripture cultivates reverence for the Lord and reminds us that we all stand equally in need of grace (Psalm 119:105; James 4:6). Pride distances us from God and from one another, but humility keeps us aligned with His ways (Proverbs 16:18; 1 Peter 5:5).

As we enter a season of fasting, God is not merely reducing our appetites; He is refining our hearts. Fasting exposes areas where we may be relying on position, experience, or self-righteousness rather than on God. Deuteronomy 17:20 calls us to walk humbly, obediently, and consistently under God’s Word, remembering that spiritual authority flows from submission to Him.

Let this fast be a time when God’s Word recenters us — keeping our hearts tender, teachable, and united. When we preserve humility, obedience follows naturally, allowing us to walk together in God’s blessing.

One Practical Step

Commit to reading the Bible daily, asking God to “...search my heart and keep me humble before You.” You can use the 365 Reading Through the Bible In A Year plan. (Available on the NECF website.)
prayers: Lord, guard my heart from pride. Help me stay committed and make reading Your Word my daily priority. Teach me how to walk humbly before You every day.
Lord, cultivate humility among Your people. Remove comparisons, divisions and self-righteousness, and clothe us with Christlike humility.
Lord, keep Your Church grounded in Your Word and help us encounter You personally every day. May our leaders and members serve with humility, unity, and obedience, bringing glory to Your name.

articles.title: The Birth of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 3: Sunday, 9 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Matthew 1:20-23

The birth of Jesus began with the annunciation to Mary by the angel Gabriel in Nazareth. The angel said she would conceive a son by the Holy Spirit and name him Jesus because He would save his people from their sins. All of this happened to fulfill the Lord’s message through the prophet Isaiah that a virgin would conceive a child and give birth to a son they would call Immanuel, which means ‘God with us.’

The idea of God becoming human is a concept that was not only foreign but also offensive to the Jews. They believed that God is spirit and thus cannot be confined to physical flesh. Moreover, because Judaism emphasises the holiness and transcendence of God, associating Him with sin, let alone with incarnation, was unthinkable.

What the Jews failed to grasp was that humility is a core attribute of God and that God, in the ultimate act of humility, would enter the world as a fragile baby in the form of Jesus. The fact that the Baby Jesus had to be totally dependent on His earthly parents compounded the matter further for them.

Christ was so humble that He willingly gave up His divine privileges to be born in human flesh and be exposed to temptation. He went to this extent because He wanted to empathise with our weaknesses. He was tempted in every way just as we are – yet He did not sin. Therefore, He was able to save us, not only from sin but also from the temptation to sin. As such, the birth of Christ is seen as God humbling Himself as a man to serve and save humanity.
prayers: Lord, I thank You for empathising with my weaknesses. You were tempted in every way; yet You did not sin. As such, You were able to save me from sin and show me the way not to sin by humbly walking in obedience to God. May I imitate Christ’s humility so that I may attain His victory.

Father, may the Church set an example of what Christ’s humility is, as a follow up of last year’s 40 Days’ Fasting and Prayer theme of Walking in the Fear of God. Let us “catch” this attitude of humility as we value others more than ourselves.
Pray that the present government of our nation remains in power so they are able to fulfil their political mandate before the country’s 16th General Elections.

articles.title: The Baptism of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 4: Monday, 10 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Matthew 3:13-16.

The Galilee region in northern Israel is famous for the Sea of Galilee which is actually a huge freshwater lake. Water from the lake flows southward into the Jordan River. Jesus lived in Nazareth, a small town in Galilee, while John was baptising people in the Jordan River near Jericho. The distance between the two places is about 130-145km.

Jesus had traveled from Galilee to the Jordan River just to be baptised by John. However, John hesitated and tried to talk Him out of it. “I am the one who needs to be baptized by You,” he said, “so why are You coming to me?”

John knew who Jesus was. When the priests and Levites had asked John who he was, John had replied, “I baptise with water, but right here in the crowd is someone you do not recognise. Though His ministry follows mine, I’m not even worthy to be His slave and untie the straps of His sandal.” The next day, when John saw Jesus coming towards him, he said, “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!”

The question is: did Jesus need to be baptised? The answer is an absolute no. Jesus was sinless and did not need to repent. Yet, He had travelled on foot for many days to be baptised by John even though He had no need of it. Then why did He do it? He did it to carry out all that God required of him. The baptism was more than just the rites. It displayed His humility in that He willingly submitted to authority though He was God incarnate.

Is it any wonder then that, as Jesus was coming up out of the water after his baptism, the heavens were opened and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and settling on Him. In the words of James 4:6 “God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble”.
prayers: Lord, I confess my spirit of insubordination. I have so often been disrespectful, disobedient, and too rebellious to submit to Your authority and instructions. I have given in to pride and arrogance rather than humility and meekness. Help me to imitate Christ’s humility to gain Your favour.
Father, help Your church to be like Jesus, who took on the very nature of a servant, chose to identify with us and surrendered His will to God.

We pray that the present coalition government will uphold the rule of the law as enshrined in the Malaysian Constitution. May there be stability that is crucial for attracting foreign investments for the future of our nation. Amen.

articles.title: The Temptation of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 5: Tuesday, 11 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Matthew 4:1-11

After Jesus had fasted for 40 days in the wilderness, Satan tempted Him to turn stones to loaves of bread, to jump off from the highest point of the Temple in Jerusalem, and to receive the kingdom of the world and all its glory. Jesus did not yield to the temptations.

Did Jesus triumph over the devil because He is God? How did the temptation show Christ’s humility?

Jesus did not use His divinity to triumph over the devil. The Scripture says, “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted there by the devil. For forty days and forty nights he fasted and became very hungry.” The Holy Spirit purposely led Jesus into temptation to show that the Son of God would remain perfectly submissive and reliant on God even under the greatest pressure. The same had happened to Moses and Elijah when they spent 40 days and nights fasting at Mount Sinai and Mount Horeb, respectively.

Jesus displayed humility when He did not respond to the devil's challenges. Yielding to the challenges and exerting His authority and power over the three temptations would have had serious consequences as it would have meant that Jesus had failed to submit to the Holy Spirit.

In the same way, when believers fail to submit to the Spirit, it reflects a lack of humility. Lucifer’s pride led to his downfall when he said, “I will ascend to heaven and set my throne above God’s stars. I will preside on the mountain of the gods far away in the north. I will climb to the highest heavens and be like the Most High.”

Christ’s humility led to His total emptying of Himself when He said, “Father, if it is Your will, take this cup away from Me; nevertheless, not My will, but Yours, be done.”
prayers: Lord, Your ways are higher than my ways and Your thoughts higher than my thoughts. I desire to follow Your example to be totally dependent on the Holy Spirit. Help me to submit to His plan and follow His instructions.
Just as Jesus emptied himself and demonstrated His selfless love, submission and obedience to God, let Your church’s attitude be the same.
Lord, may You uphold peace and harmony in our coalition government and its opposition. May all parties prioritise maintaining a good working relationship for the wellbeing of all Malaysians.

articles.title: The Welcoming Humility of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 6: Wednesday, 12 August 2026
articles.content:
Mark 10:13–16 (NIV)

“And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them and blessed them.”

Jesus’ time on earth was short. There was much to do. Places to go and people to meet. Surely a good strategy would be to maximise His time with the important people of His day - the movers and the shakers of society. As conventional wisdom would say, “Your network is your net-worth.” But Christ was anything but conventional. He did the unexpected: He made sure to stop and spend time with children.

The disciples tried sending the children away, but Jesus rebuked them. In a move that must have surprised everyone, He welcomed the children, blessed them and even said, “the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.”

Such as these? These mischievous kids running around? Yes. While others saw children as unimportant, Christ saw them as wonderful citizens of His everlasting Kingdom. Each of them was a precious child of God in His eyes. Little ones were to be loved and embraced, not ignored.

Which begs the questions: How do we treat the little, the lost and the lowly among us? Those whom society deem unimportant? Have we ignored them? Do we make time for them or are we too caught up with our own sense of self-importance? Our Great King, in His humility, stooped down and welcomed them into His open arms. May we do likewise.
prayers: Pray that, as we pursue the mind of Christ, the door of wisdom would open up the importance of seeking favour and true relationship with God. The humility that we learn from our interaction with children reflects the reality of our net-worth.

Pray that we would learn from children about humility, especially when forgiveness is frequently practised. Even when we disagree as adults, there is always room to share our thoughts, without argument or stubbornness.
Pray that the recent launch of the new education policy will be passionately and zealously embraced by teachers. Immediate results are not expected but their faithful execution will bear much fruit.

articles.title: The Serving Humility of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 7: Thursday, 13 August 2026
articles.content:
Matthew 21:1-5 (NIV)

5 “Say to Daughter Zion,
 ‘See, your king comes to you,
gentle and riding on a donkey,
 and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”

The final week leading up to our Lord’s crucifixion is known as the Passion Week. Today the word “passion” usually means to have strong feelings. But if you would go back to its roots, the word passion comes from the Latin passio, which carries the meaning of “suffering” or “enduring.” To suffer is one thing; to do so willingly is another. The latter requires great humility.

How did the Passion Week begin? It began with Christ riding into Jerusalem on a donkey. In biblical times, kings could choose to either ride on a horse or a donkey. The animal of choice would reflect the purpose that the king had in mind. Horses were mostly associated with war, power and military conquest. On the other hand, donkeys were chosen for times of peace and portrayed humility.

In fulfillment of the prophecy, Christ chose a donkey. And the symbolism was clear - Christ had come not to dominate but to serve. Not to destroy but to bring peace. Not to seize power but to submit to the Father’s will. What Christ taught, He himself lived. “Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all (Mark 10:43b-44).”

How about us today? In a world where often “might makes right”, and we are told to “win at all cost” and to “crush the competition,” could the words of Christ be inviting us to another way? A way that chooses the donkey over the horse. A way of giving oneself in service of others. Daunting, isn’t it? Because it seems disadvantageous - we might lose out. But Christ did promise, “the meek shall inherit the earth (Matt. 5:5),” And we do good to remember Christ shall return, not on a donkey, but victorious on a white horse (see Rev. 19:11).
prayers: The desire to be humble comes with a price and our Lord has demonstrated how to endure and suffer. Let’s pray that we would learn from the Lord on allowing humility to shine in our lives.

Let’s pray that we would do everything without complaining or arguing. As God’s children we desire to be blameless and pure in a crooked and depraved generation. Jesus chose a donkey instead of a horse, a way of giving oneself in service of others.

Corruption in the form of financial leakage has been reported every year by the Government Audit Department. Pray for wisdom to implement safety measures to reduce such losses and make those in power accountable.

articles.title: The Feet-Washing Humility of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 8: Friday, 14 August 2026
articles.content:
John 13:1 -17 (NIV)

“After that, he poured water into a basin and began to wash his disciples’ feet, …”

The night before Jesus was crucified stands out like a candle in the dark, showing us His great humility more clearly than any other moment. Here in today’s reading, we see the disciples gathered for the Last Supper. It was here that Christ would do the unimaginable.

No one could have foreseen this. Foot washing was normally a servant's job. But here, Christ used it to reveal the driving force behind everything he did. What was it? It was the heart of humility. In Christ's own words “For the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).”

Imagine that. Almighty God, Creator of Heaven and Earth, the one who holds the universe in the palm of His hands - stooping down to wash the feet of people made from the dust of the earth. It is hard to fully grasp. But as we reflect on it, the more we realize we are called to follow in our Lord’s footsteps - serving others in the name of Christ.
articles.reflection: If you knew death awaited you the very next day - what would be the last thing you would do? What would be the enduring lesson you would want to impart? And how would you impart it? After all, there are many virtues in our faith that are worth passing on. Of all things, Christ chose to wash His disciples’ feet.
prayers: Bearing in mind the feet-washing demonstration by Jesus towards his disciples, let’s pray that as Christians, we are reminded that we have been called to serve rather than to be served.
Pray that we will make a difference in a world where self-preservation and self-gratification are placed above all else.

Structural reform and good governance can boost the integrity of our civil service when the public provides constructive suggestions on areas of improvement. Let’s pray Malaysians will depart from a culture of chronic complaining and begin to engage our Government with constructive feedback.

articles.title: The Silent Humility of Christ
articles.subtitle: Day 9: Saturday, 15 August 2026
articles.content:
Matthew 26:57–63a (NIV)

“But Jesus remained silent.”

The closer we get to the crucifixion, the more we see the humility of Christ unfolding. Arrested and put before the Sanhedrin, Jesus had all the right to defend himself against the false accusations. Jesus could have threatened, called down judgment, or simply crushed humanity in an instant. Yet Jesus chose the path of silence (vs.63).

Silent. Like a lamb led to the slaughter. He said nothing to vindicate himself. He did nothing to force the outcome. Why? Because Christ had already surrendered His life into the hands of the Father, saying, “...yet not my will but Yours be done (Luke 22:42b, NIV).” The will of the Father was for Him to die for the sins of man. And so, Christ silently stood with only the cruel cross ahead. But who could have known that this path of humility would become the path to glory?

The Apostle Paul describes it best: “[Jesus] humbled himself by becoming obedient to death—even death on a cross! Therefore God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil 2:8b-9, NIV).”

What a glorious mystery: Christ’s humiliation was Christ’s exaltation. It was His humility that defeated the boast of the last enemy - death. In this we can rejoice, for our Great King humbled Himself to be like us, that we might become like Him. And at the end of days, the silence shall be broken as the heavens declare, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and He shall reign forever and ever” (Rev. 11:15, NKJV). Until then, we wait with humble hearts.
prayers: As we live in obedience to God, we should never think that we have arrived or that we are superior to others. Like a lamb led to the slaughter, Jesus said nothing to vindicate himself. As God works in us, let us desire to do His will.
Humility is not self-degrading or self-despising. Pray that the needs and interests of others be brought to the forefront for our Lord is the silent listener in all our conversations.

The Government has successfully launched a few initiatives to help the people cope with rising costs of living. Pray for wisdom to ensure these schemes would certainly benefit those in both the B40* and M40* categories.
The term B40 stands for Bottom 40% of income earners in Malaysia and is part of a broader classification system that includes M40 (Middle 40%) and T20 (Top 20%).

articles.title: Examining the Roots of Pride
articles.subtitle: Day 10: Sunday, 16 August 2026
articles.content:
James 4:6 (NIV)

“God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble.”

As we enter the second week of prayer and fasting, we turn our attention to the characteristics of humility. Humility is not merely an outward posture or polite behaviour; it is a condition of the heart that shapes how we relate to God, others, and ourselves. At its opposite stands pride—a subtle yet destructive force that can take root in every aspect of life.

Pride expresses itself in many forms: self-sufficiency in our spiritual life, defensiveness in relationships, the desire for recognition in ministry, resistance to correction, and the quiet confidence that we know better than God. Often, pride hides beneath religious activity, competence, or even good intentions. This makes it especially dangerous, for it can exist undetected unless we intentionally examine our hearts.

Scripture reminds us that God actively resists the proud. This is a sobering truth. Pride not only distances us from others; it disrupts our fellowship with God. Humility, on the other hand, opens the way for grace—grace to repent, grace to change, and grace to grow.

This week invites us to allow the Holy Spirit to search us deeply. As we fast, we are called to confront pride in every sphere of life—our personal spirituality, family relationships, leadership responsibilities, ministry service, and public witness. True humility begins when we acknowledge our need for God in everything and surrender every area of self-rule to Him.
articles.reflection: In which areas of your life might pride be subtly shaping your attitudes or actions?
prayers: Lord, search my heart and reveal any pride that resists Your rule. Teach me to walk humbly before You in every area of my life. As I fast and pray, form in me a heart that welcomes Your grace.
Lord, help Your Church to embrace humility as an elusive trait, where You get all the credit for choosing us so we boast only in You.
As the economic outlook for 2026 appears to be very challenging; let’s pray for wisdom upon our national leadership to navigate and manage the country’s resources efficiently.

articles.title: Dependence on God
articles.subtitle: Day 11: Monday, 17 August 2026
articles.content:
Proverbs 3:5 (NIV)

“Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding.” One defining characteristic of humility is dependence on God. Pride teaches us to rely on our own strength, experience, and ability. Humility acknowledges our limitations and chooses trust.

Many church leaders burn out not because they lack calling or commitment, but because they carry the weight of ministry alone. When dependence shifts from God to self, prayer becomes secondary, rest feels like weakness, and outcomes feel like personal responsibility. Over time, this silent self-reliance drains the soul.

A person who truly depends on God looks different. They pray before they act. They listen before they decide. They are willing to say “I don’t know” and “I need help.” They embrace God’s timing rather than force results. Their confidence is not in efficiency or competence, but in God’s faithfulness.

Dependence on God does not lead to passivity; it leads to obedience. It frees us from striving and invites us to serve with joy rather than pressure. Fasting reminds us that life and ministry are sustained not by human effort, but by God’s sustaining grace.

As we examine our hearts this week, we must ask whether our busyness masks pride, and whether our strength has replaced surrender.
articles.reflection: In your responsibilities and ministry, are you relying more on God’s strength or your own ability?
prayers: Father, forgive me for the times I have depended on myself instead of You. Teach me to trust You fully, to pray continually, and to rest in Your sufficiency. Renew my strength as I learn to walk humbly with You.
Lord, teach Your church to happily admit that everything we have is a free gift from God, so that we can’t boast in it, much less be arrogant in it.
We pray the Government machinery will be alert and flexible in implementing changes in the light of a rapidly-changing and challenging world.

articles.title: A Teachable and Discerning Heart
articles.subtitle: Day 12: Tuesday, 18 August 2026
articles.content:
Proverbs 12:15 (NIV)

“The way of fools seems right to them, but the wise listen to advice.”

A humble heart is a teachable heart. Pride resists correction because of the fear of being exposed. Humility, however, is the willingness to be corrected, to admit, “I am wrong,” and to grow from honest feedback. This is not weakness—it is spiritual maturity.

Over time, it can become harder for the heart to remain teachable. As we grow accustomed to our habits, opinions, and ways of doing things, we can become comfortable—even rigid. What once was discernment slowly turns into assumption. What once was conviction becomes routine. Without humility, our patterns can harden into spiritual blindness.

God often speaks through people around us—leaders, colleagues, family members, and even those who disagree with us. A humble person listens carefully, weighs feedback prayerfully, and resists the urge to defend or justify too quickly. At the same time, humility requires a discerning heart that listens not only to human voices but also to the gentle prompting of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit convicts, guides, and redirects us so that we remain aligned with God’s will.

In this season of fasting and prayer, we must ask God to soften our hearts. Are we still willing to be taught? Are we still willing to change? Humility keeps us responsive to God and open to transformation.
articles.reflection: When was the last time you received a correction without becoming defensive?
prayers: Lord, give me a humble and discerning heart. Help me to accept correction, to admit when I am wrong, and to listen to the guidance of Your Spirit. Break every pattern of pride that keeps me from growing.

Humility teaches us to acknowledge that You alone govern our every heartbeat and the outcome of our endeavours—whether we arrive safely or not. Lord, we depend entirely on You and desire to remain in Your will.

Pray for our Government to have wisdom to manage the climate changes that affect the economy. May they make serious decisions for the survival of all citizens, free from the biasness of race and religion.

articles.title: Antidote for Pride
articles.subtitle: Day 13: Wednesday, 19 August 2026
articles.content:
Deuteronomy 17:18-20 (NLT)

18 “When he sits on the throne as king, he must copy for himself this body of instruction on a scroll in the presence of the Levitical priests. 19 He must always keep that copy with him and read it daily as long as he lives. That way he will learn to fear the LORD his God by obeying all the terms of these instructions and decrees. 20 This regular reading will prevent him from becoming proud and acting as if he is above his fellow citizens. It will also prevent him from turning away from these commands in the smallest way. And it will ensure that he and his descendants will reign for many generations in Israel.”

Pride can creep up on us very subtly. If we don’t guard ourselves against this sin, Satan will use it not only to destroy us, but also to destroy our witness to our families and those who look to us as role models in their quest to follow Jesus.

One antidote to this insidious sin is found in Deuteronomy 17:18-20, particularly verse 20. The consistent habit of reading God’s Word - if done with a desire to love God and our neighbours - will also help us fulfill our desire to walk humbly before Him.
prayers: Pray that believers who walk in the corridors of power would be able to guard their hearts against the sin of pride. God had established this concern even before the first king of Israel was chosen.
Jesus in Matthew 20.25 warned against"lording it over"others. Pray that God’s leaders would lead with sacrificial care for others, and depart from exerting domineering control for selfish gain.
Pray for our nation’s elected leaders to remember they were voted into power to represent the interest and concerns of the rakyat and not to forward their personal agenda.

articles.title: What is in Our Hearts?
articles.subtitle: Day 14: Thursday, 20 August 2026
articles.content:
Jeremiah 17:9-10 (NKJV)
9 “The heart is deceitful above all things,
And desperately wicked;
Who can know it?
10 I, the LORD, search the heart,
I test the mind,
Even to give every man according to his ways,
According to the fruit of his doings.”

Yesterday we looked at how God helps us walk humbly before Him. Today we look at another way He does this: by allowing us to go through challenges and humiliating situations to see how we respond.

These tests may come through how we are treated or served; when we are criticised or ridiculed; honored or respected; or when we are overlooked for a promotion.

When such humiliating situations take place, God uses them to expose what is truly in our hearts and minds through our words and deeds.

How we respond to God and to those who humiliate us is crucial. Our reaction determines our Heavenly Father’s next course of action, as His desire is for us to become more like Jesus. See Philippians 2:1-8.
prayers: During Israel's 40 years of wandering in the wilderness, God assured them of His constant presence. Jesus gave his disciples the Great Commission and reaffirmed this covenant in Matthew 28:20b “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Pray that we would know His abiding presence.

In our spiritual journey trials and testing will come along the way to sharpen, humiliate and challenge. Here is where our eyes need to be fixed upon Jesus the Author and Perfecter of our faith. Pray for strength to endure and overcome.

Politicians often have a hard time gaining credibility in the eyes of the people. Christian politicians are not exempted from this stigmatisation. Pray that Christian politicians will fear God and walk closely with Him. Identify them by name.

articles.title: He Moulds the Heart
articles.subtitle: Day 15: Friday, 21 August 2026
articles.content:
Psalms 105:17-19 (NLT)
17 Then he sent someone to Egypt ahead of them—
Joseph, who was sold as a slave.
18 They bruised his feet with fetters
and placed his neck in an iron collar.
19 Until the time came to fulfill his dreams,
the LORD tested Joseph’s character.

Genesis 37:5-8 (NLT)
5 One night Joseph had a dream, and when he told his brothers about it, they hated him more than ever. 6 “Listen to this dream,” he said. 7 “We were out in the field, tying up bundles of grain. Suddenly my bundle stood up, and your bundles all gathered around and bowed low before mine!”
8 His brothers responded, “So you think you will be our king, do you? Do you actually think you will reign over us?” And they hated him all the more because of his dreams and the way he talked about them.

Yesterday we learned that God will “search the heart and test the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10a.)

A powerful example of this is found in the life of Joseph, whose story is found in Genesis 37 and 39-50. Interestingly, 12 chapters - or more than 20% of the book of Genesis - are dedicated to his life.

A large portion of this narrative focuses on the humbling process Joseph had to go through before God could use him to fulfil His divine plan and destiny.

Ultimately, Joseph's final response to these trials revealed the true state of his heart. See Genesis 50:14-21.
prayers: As God’s people many times we have often been misunderstood for doing the right thing. Pray for their protection and encourage them to look to God as what Abraham in Genesis 18:25 asked"Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?".

Pray for the Lord to prepare the younger generation, who may say the wrong things and yet are not aware “that God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive” (Genesis 50:20)

Difficult days are looming in the horizon and national decisions taken may be unpleasant. Pray that national leaders will close government institutions/companies that are draining the states’ financial resources.

articles.title: Submission with Discernment
articles.subtitle: Day 16: Saturday, 22 August 2026
articles.content:
1 Peter 2:13 (NIV)

“Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human authority...” One important expression of humility is submission to authority. In a culture that celebrates independence and self-assertion, Scripture calls us to practise submission as a spiritual discipline. Whether in the church, the workplace, or the family, humility recognises that God works through order, leadership, and accountability.

However, biblical submission is not blind obedience. Our ultimate loyalty is to God. When something seems wrong, unjust, or contrary to God’s truth, humility does not remain silent—but it speaks with gentleness and respect. Pride reacts with anger or rebellion; humility responds with courage out of love.

James reminds us to be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry” (James 1:19). A humble heart seeks first to understand before demanding to be understood. It listens carefully, discerns prayerfully, and then speaks wisely. This posture protects relationships while still honouring truth.

Submission shaped by humility does not mean suppressing conviction. It means trusting God enough to express concerns without bitterness, manipulation, or fear. When our hearts are anchored in obedience to God, we can relate to authority with both faithfulness and integrity.

As we fast and pray, may God teach us to live under His lordship in every relationship.
articles.reflection: Do you respond to authority with humility, discernment, and respect?
prayers: Lord, teach me to submit with wisdom and grace. Help me to listen well, speak gently, and obey You above all else. Form in me a humble spirit that honours You in every relationship.

As C.S. Lewis said,"Humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less."Humility does not mean weakness or self-hatred. Lord, help us to be humble in relationship with You and have strength under control.

articles.title: Humility Enables Us to Rely More Fully on God
articles.subtitle: Day 17: Sunday, 23 August 2026
articles.content:
1 Timothy 1:16 (RSV)

“But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life.”

Truly spiritual characters in the Bible share a defining hallmark: a humility that is as genuine as it is absolute. A. W. Tozer, the American spiritual writer and theologian, once expressed it well: “Humility is not a behaviour, but an attitude — the recognition that all the good we possess comes from God.”

As a towering figure of the New Testament, Paul stood as a once-in-an-era apostle and God’s masterpiece, specially ordained as a chosen vessel for His purposes. Once a violent persecutor of Jesus’ followers, Paul was transformed by an encounter with the Lord on the road to Damascus. His life thereafter was one marked by deep repentance, humility, and unwavering obedience as he served the Lord faithfully and followed Him closely.

Paul’s humility led him to clearly recognise his own weaknesses and limitations, compelling him to rely even more on God. He performed miracles, wrote epistles, and established churches, yet still emphasised that he was the “chief of sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Among his many admirable traits, of supreme importance was his complete humility and obedience. He frequently minimised his own status, referring to himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ”, “the least of all the saints”, “unworthy to be called an apostle”, and “the chief of sinners”. These heartfelt confessions can only flow from a spirit of true humility and submission. Such humility deepens our dependence on our Lord for His help and guidance, so that His perfect will may be accomplished on earth through our lives
prayers: Lord, shine Your light on the areas where we still cling to our own opinions or doubts. Help us to lay aside ourselves and trust in You wholeheartedly.
Lord, remind us that we are sinners saved by grace. May we remain humble in Christ and walk closely with You.

Pray that steps be taken to review the Malaysian Education policy, with intention to produce good citizens for the future who will be able to face the challenging demands of the world. The nation’s survival is of utmost importance.

articles.title: Humility Fosters Better Relationships
articles.subtitle: Day 18: Monday, 24 August 2026
articles.content:
1 Corinthians 10:23–24 (RSV)

“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbour.

Augustine, the renowned theologian of the medieval period, once famously remarked: “If you ask me what is the most important virtue in the Christian life, I would reply: first, humility; second, humility; third, still humility.” Humility is the first step in serving the Lord, and is also the most important one. It promotes harmony in human relationships and makes people easier to get along with. A humble person does not make others feel pressured or belittled; rather, they are more willing to listen, are skilled at cooperation, and are more likely to earn trust.

Truly influential leaders are not arrogant; they are humble. Humility encourages people to value relationships, work well in teams, and accept different ideas and perspectives. These leaders build their influence by serving and helping others, rather than by simply using their power or authority. As Paul says: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbour. (1 Corinthians 10:23–24) When a leader is relationship-centred and God-centred, they earn the respect and trust of those they lead. On the other hand, proud people often have no reverence for God and do not care about others, which causes arguments and tension in relationships. Because of this, a humble heart is indispensable for getting along well with everyone.
prayers: Lord, remove all pride from our hearts and help us to value our relationship with You and with others.

Lord, teach us to treat everyone with a humble heart. Instead of focusing only on our own interests, teach us to truly care about the needs and feelings of those around us, just as Jesus showed us by putting others first with His self-giving love.

The small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have been the backbone of the Malaysian economy for years. It has created employment, stabilised businesses and strengthened working relationships among races. Pray that the government provides creative incentives for SMEs to sustain growth.

articles.title: Humility Enables People to Value Peace and Prioritise the Bigger Picture
articles.subtitle: Day 19: Tuesday, 25 August 2026
articles.content:
Numbers 12:3

“Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.”

Hudson Taylor once said, “God is looking for weak and humble people so that His power may be revealed.” Humility occupies a central place in the Christian life and ministry, and it often brings a series of blessings to one’s spiritual life. A humble person is aware of their own limitations, does not let their successes make them self-satisfied, and is eager to listen to others, keep learning new things, and continue to grow and be renewed.

Moses is a prime example of such a person. While leading millions of Israelites out of Egypt, he bore immense leadership pressure and faced criticism from all sides. He had to endure not only the people’s continual complaints (Numbers 13:1–3; 14:1–10), but also attacks from his own sister Miriam and brother Aaron (Numbers 12:1–10). Yet Moses did not defend himself. Instead, with a gentle heart, he entrusted everything to God and waited for Him to handle the situation. Instead of relying on his own experience or authority, he submitted to God’s guidance and faced the hardships and challenges of the Exodus journey willingly.

Humble people can step back and see the big picture instead of worrying about their pride and status. This helps them resolve conflicts and bring about solutions more effectively. For example, even amid repeated leadership crises, Moses chose to walk humbly with God and to give all the glory entirely to Him. No wonder Scripture describes him in these words: “Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3)
prayers: Lord, help us to recognise our limitations. Grant us teachable hearts, so that we may learn humbly from others and never hesitate to ask for guidance.

Lord, let us in humility consider others better than ourselves, not doing anything out of our selfish ambition or vain conceit. May we look not only to our own interests, but also to the interests of others.

The Madani Government’s actions and attitude today is crucial in setting the tone for the succeeding government. Pray that peace and harmony can be witnessed all across Malaysia’s Civil Services support.

articles.title: Humility Makes It Easier to Obey God and Be Mightily Used by Him
articles.subtitle: Day 20: Wednesday, 26 August 2026
articles.content:
Genesis 41:16

Joseph answered Pharaoh, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favourable answer.”

George Müller once said, “The vessel God uses must be a humble vessel.” On a spiritual level, humility brings great benefit. Humility enables a person to obey God’s leading more readily, and to see God’s work rather than their own performance. A humble person does not need to compete at every turn or constantly try to prove that they are better than others. Because of that, their hearts are lighter, they have less anxiety, and their faith is greater. Such a humble life often brings about profound spiritual transformation, making it one that God delights in and chooses to use as a leader.

One classic example in the Bible of such a person is Joseph. At the age of seventeen, Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers. He later faced more hardship when he was falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife and thrown into prison, where he was even forgotten by the cupbearer whom he had helped when he interpreted his dream. Yet because of his humble obedience, God never stopped watching over him. When he finally stood before Pharaoh to explain a dream, Joseph gave all the glory to God for his wisdom, saying, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favourable answer” (Genesis 41:16).

Even after Joseph was promoted to a position of great power as the governor of Egypt, he still treated with gentleness and kindness the very brothers who had once humiliated, harmed, and sold him into slavery (see Genesis 37:18–36). In spite of it all, there was no bitterness, hatred, or desire for revenge in his heart (50:15–21). This is the beautiful spiritual fruit borne of humility—it allows a person to trust completely that God is still in control of everything. As John Calvin noted, “True humility is forgetting oneself and fixing one’s eyes on the glory of God.” It is the choice to give all glory to God rather than to oneself, to submit willingly to His leading, to rejoice in the fulfilment of His will, and to be willing to be used by the Lord.
prayers: Lord, soften our hardened hearts; make us gentle, teachable, and willing to be shaped by You. Help us to fully follow Your lead.
Lord, remove the pride within us. Help us to work out our salvation with fear and trembling. We seek not our own glory, but are willing to become vessels fit for use in Your hands.

articles.title: The Humble Enjoy Rest
articles.subtitle: Day 21: Thursday, 27 August 2026
articles.content:
Matthew 11:28–29 (RSV)

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

The Lord Jesus invites us - His people - to find true rest for our souls. He calls us to stop struggling under the heavy weight of trying to handle life on our own and instead to live each day filled with His peace and lightness of heart.

If we are gentle and humble, we will be freed from the crushing pressures of the world upon our souls. We would no longer have to carry the exhausting and unbearable burdens of constant comparison, the anxiety of calculating our gains and losses, and the endless rivalries that only clutter our heart and steal our joy. If we refuse to let go and insist on going our own way, we will miss the true inner peace and happiness that come only through contentment and gratitude.

Let us learn gentleness and humility from the Lord, firmly trusting in the Father’s promises, and resting in faith. Dwell in the Father’s presence, knowing that He knows all things, and that we need not cling to grievances because of that. Even in circumstances that seem hopeless, we can remain at peace because we are confident that our heavenly Father reigns and rules over all. We belong to Him; He is the Lord God.

The humble and gentle rest quietly in His love—secure, and unafraid of storms or attacks. He calms our hearts and grants us rest. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” (Psalm 46:1). Humility and gentleness enable us to enjoy rest and in that security and serenity, we will know, see, and experience God’s presence.
prayers: Oh Lord, what wealth of peace we forfeit when our days are filled with the tyranny of busyness! Teach us to value the precious moments of being still before You and hearing from You.
Lord, we bring the needs and interests of others to the forefront. It is not self-degradation on our part; it causes our focus to expand beyond ourselves and our minds to consider others.

articles.title: The Gentle Obtain Harmony and Peace
articles.subtitle: Day 22: Friday, 28 August 2026
articles.content:
Matthew 5:5 (RSV)

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

Philippians 4:5

“Let your reasonableness be known to everyone.”

Read Genesis 26:12–33

Isaac is a model of humility and peace. He had inherited the blessing God gave to his forefather Abraham, and was content and secure in what he had received. Despite facing constant mistreatment, he maintained a humble and gentle attitude. When the Philistines became jealous of him and destroyed his possessions, he did not dwell on the injustice. Rooted in humility, he chose to generously surrender the land that was rightfully his.

Isaac never grew discouraged or gave up. He re-dug wells; and when they were seized again, he did not quarrel but just dug another. Isaac's humble obedience eventually led to the fulfillment of the promise: “For now the Lord has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.” By refusing to strive and by remaining gentle, he was granted an even broader space and greater growth.

Through Isaac, people saw his God and his faith. Those who are humble and peace-loving allow others to see that “those who trust in God have peace in their hearts and are children of peace.” Abimelech declared to Isaac, “We see plainly that the Lord has been with you.” (v. 28), and therefore made a covenant of peace with him.

God Himself appeared to Isaac and promised him great blessing.

The gentle possess inner peace. They remain steady amid adversity, and life flourishes wherever they go.
prayers: Lord Jesus, this day I choose patience and kindness over strife and competition. Broaden my mind and heart to understand and live out Your compassion and generosity.

Lord, give us the peace-loving humility that shines in the darkness, not because we are self-promoting, but because we have died to self and are living in Christ. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

The increasing use of hate speech in social media platforms is instigating conflict between the different races. It has been difficult for parties to mediate or reconcile their differences. Pray for more regulation processes over this.

articles.title: The Humble are Wise
articles.subtitle: Day 23: Saturday, 29 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Psalm 131

The meek will inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace. (Psalm 37:11)

Deuteronomy 33:25

“Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be” (Deuteronomy 33:25).

A humble attitude before God acknowledges that His sovereign will is higher and that His plans are more profound. A heart steeped in arrogance and proud eyes obscure the vision of God, leaving souls lost and confused.

The truly humble wait patiently upon God. When faced with matters too great and beyond their understanding, they refuse to act rashly. Acting independently of God’s guidance often leads to a cycle of fruitless effort and deep discouragement.

The humble bow low in surrender, aligning themselves with the Lord, and abiding in His presence. As a result, their hearts become still and calm. Those who are secure in the Lord are gentle in spirit and clear in vision.

The humble look to God and therefore see higher and farther.

The humble are wise.
prayers: Lord, as we lift up our eyes to You, may we catch a glimpse of Your greatness; and pour disdain on our pride and feeble efforts to attain Your acceptance outside the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Pray that we check our motives when we share our opinions and feelings, that we do not show how great we are, but to hear the Lord’s voice so that we are able to express that love and promote unity.

articles.content: Hindrances to Humility

articles.title: Pride of Self-Sufficiency
articles.subtitle: Day 24: Sunday, 30 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Deuteronomy 8:17–18; John 15:5

One of the most subtle enemies of humility is self-sufficiency—the belief that life, progress, and fruitfulness are sustained by our own strength. Moses warned Israel that prosperity can quietly distort memory, leading the heart to say, “My power and the strength of my hands have produced this…” (Deut. 8:17, NIV).

This form of pride is rarely loud. It often hides behind competence, experience, and success. Jesus exposes the illusion plainly: “...apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). He reminds us that breath, wisdom, endurance, and spiritual fruit are not self-generated; they are sustained by God’s grace.

Self-sufficiency slowly displaces prayer. Dependence is replaced by control, intimacy by activity. Over time, this produces exhaustion, spiritual dullness, and a quiet drift from God.

How do we overcome self-sufficiency?

By intentionally re-anchoring our lives in dependence on God. True humility is not thinking less of ourselves, but remembering God rightly. Being grateful recentres the heart. Prayer then evolves from a last-resort desperation into a continual alignment with His will. In fasting, we confront the illusion of control and return to daily reliance on God’s sustaining grace.
prayers: Lord, deliver me from the illusion that I can carry my life without You. Teach me again to depend on You. I confess how easily I rely on my own strength and forget Your sustaining grace. Teach me again to depend on You for life, wisdom, and fruitfulness. Strip away my self-reliance and restore a childlike trust in my heart. I choose dependence, not independence.
Lord, guard my heart against self-centredness, envy and jealousy so that I will not resent the success of others that will destroy true relationships both with You and men.

The government has less than two years to fulfil their Reform Checklist to the Rakyat. With the fragile coalition, pray that the PM will not accede to political compromises in order to gain support for coming GE16 in 2027.

articles.title: Let’s Not Forget
articles.subtitle: Day 25: Monday, 31 August 2026
articles.content:
Read Psalm 90:9, 10; Jeremiah 29:10; Daniel 9:2; Luke 10

Sixty-nine years ago, our forefathers, led by Tunku Abdul Rahman, gathered at Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur and shouted “Merdeka!”* seven times. This was the perfect proclamation of a new, fledgling and independent federation - Malaya - carrying the promise of freedom, unity and a commitment to a just and inclusive society for every citizen. Sabah and Sarawak joined the federation as equal partners to form the nation of Malaysia in 1963.

Next year, Malaysia enters her 70th year of Merdeka. In Scripture, the number 70 signifies perfection, completion and also judgment. Moses wrote that man’s lifespan - denoting fullness - is 70 years (Psalm 90:9, 10); God promised Israel would return from exile after 70 years (Jeremiah 29:10, Daniel 9:2); and Christ sent out 70 disciples to heal the sick and preach the Gospel of the kingdom in the towns (Luke 10). As our nation celebrates this landmark year, let’s not forget our humble origins, nor our forefathers’ contribution that built this country from a distant backwater to where we are today.

Malaysia now stands as a sovereign nation whose unique formation is unlike any other. We have evolved from a bustling entrepot in the late Middle Ages to a colonial outpost, and now to a modern metropolis celebrated for our rich cultural diversity and historical significance. The road to nationhood, however, is long and fraught with challenges. While every Malaysian may be proud - in a good way - to identify with our land; we realise that meekness and lowliness of spirit remain a vital part of national unity. As believers, we are reminded to model Christ’s humility among people of different races, cultures and religions in our expression of merdeka.
prayers: If you are Malaysian, give thanks for being born in this country of milk and honey. If you are not Malaysian, give thanks for the opportunity to be here, sharing the warmth and goodness of the nation.

The Malaysian Church has existed longer than the Merdeka 70 years that we are in today. We are the bride of our Lord Jesus Christ. Is the Bridegroom pleased with the state of the church? Let us repent for our shortcomings and pray for the Lord’s grace and mercy.

As a nation we have come a long way compared with our neighbours, albeit there is no comparison with Singapore! However, if we continue to be complacent and careless, we can slide backwards to third-world-nation status. Let us strive to be a nation of milk and honey.

articles.title: Fear of People
articles.subtitle: Day 26: Tuesday, 1 September 2026
articles.content:
Read Proverbs 29:25; Galatians 1:10

Pride does not always look like arrogance. It often hides as approval-seeking. Scripture calls this the fear of man—shaping our choices around human affirmation rather than obedience to God.

Proverbs warns, “Fear of man will prove to be a snare…” (Prov. 29:25, NIV). When approval becomes central, humility collapses into performance. Convictions are edited, obedience becomes selective, and faithfulness is measured by applause rather than truth.

Paul speaks clearly: “If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10b). To fear people is not humility; it is misplaced allegiance. True humility flows from reverence for God above all other voices.

How do we overcome fear of man?

By re-centering our identity in Christ. When we know who we belong to, we no longer need to belong to everyone. The fear of the Lord realigns courage, clarity, and obedience. Fasting quiets competing voices and restores God’s authority at the centre of our lives.
prayers: Lord, free me from the prison of people-pleasing. Teach me to fear You rightly. I surrender my need for approval and the fear of human opinion. Anchor my identity in Your love and truth. Give me the courage to obey You even when it costs me. May reverence for You outweigh every other voice.

John 15:5 affirms that Jesus is the source of life, and believers are connected to Him just as branches are to a vine. Pray for a deep and continuous fellowship with Jesus whom we acknowledge as the Source of our spiritual nourishment. Apart from Him we can do nothing.

Two important reforms mentioned were the Political Financing Act and the separation of power between Attorney-General and the Public Prosecutor. Initiating these reforms would be a milestone for the present Government. Pray that they be granted courage and wisdom to implement the many reforms.

articles.title: Spiritual Comparison
articles.subtitle: Day 27: Wednesday, 2 September 2026
articles.content:
Read Luke 18:9–14; 2 Corinthians 10:12

Few things undermine humility faster than comparison. Jesus exposes this in the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector. One measured himself against others; the other stood honestly before God. Only one went home justified.

Comparison shifts our gaze to the side rather than upward. Paul warns that those who compare themselves with others “...are not wise” (2 Cor. 10:12). Comparison produces pride when we feel superior, and despair when we feel inferior—but both are centred on self rather than God.

Humility is not found by ranking ourselves accurately, but by standing truthfully before the Lord.

How do we overcome the urge to compare?

By returning to honest prayer. The tax collector’s cry—“God, have mercy on me”—restores humility. When grace becomes our reference point, comparison loses its grip. Fasting strips away external measurements and brings us back to God alone, where true transformation begins.
prayers: Lord, deliver me from comparing my journey with others. Teach me to walk faithfully in my calling. I lay down comparison and self-measurement before You. Cleanse my heart from pride, envy, and insecurity. Teach me to stand honestly before You, not against others. Shape me by Your grace, not by comparison.

Pride is the primary hindrance to humility, manifesting self-centeredness, arrogance and seeking praise. Pray that we will be able to recognise these threats and stay on course in the race that the Lord has set before us.
Pray for the Ministry of Finance (MOF) to be given boldness to bring down the national debt even though the nation has to face strong geopolitical headwinds at the economic front.

articles.title: An Unteachable Spirit
articles.subtitle: Day 28: Thursday, 3 September 2026
articles.content:
Read Proverbs 12:15; James 1:21

Pride often reveals itself through an unteachable spirit. Proverbs warns, “The way of fools seems right to them…” (Prov. 12:15, NIV). An unteachable heart resists correction, resents feedback, and is under the delusion that one is spiritually or personally mature enough to refuse to be under anyone’s authority.

James urges believers to receive the Word with humility (James 1:21). Teachability is not a weakness; it is spiritual strength. It requires listening, restraint, and a willingness to be shaped by truth.

An unteachable spirit does not lack information—it resists surrender.

How do we overcome an unteachable spirit?

By cultivating a posture of listening. Humility asks, “Lord, what am I not seeing?” Fasting slows the soul, softens defensiveness, and creates space for God’s Word to correct and transform us. Grace flows where openness remains.
prayers: Lord, soften my heart. Make me teachable again. Holy Spirit, soften my heart and quiet my defensiveness. Give me ears to hear and a heart willing to be corrected. Remove pride that resists instruction and truth. Form in me a teachable, obedient spirit.

In John 5:44 Jesus warns us about our desire of receiving honour and praise from each other rather than seeking approval from God alone. Pray that our greatest desire would be changed to seek honour that comes from God only.

As much as the government desires to push for growth, it must not allow sentiment to cloud their decisions to first implement key reforms. With a challenging world economy, there will be no room for margin of error in this regard.

articles.title: Resentment and Unforgiveness
articles.subtitle: Day 29: Friday, 4 September 2026
articles.content:
Read Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:31–32

Pride often survives through resentment. Unforgiveness quietly declares, “I deserve better.” Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant shows how forgetting mercy hardens the heart.

Paul reminds us to forgive as the Lord forgave us (Eph. 4:32). Humility remembers the grace we have received, not merely the wrongs we have suffered. Unforgiveness keeps us elevated above others; forgiveness brings us back to the level ground of the cross.

How do we overcome unforgiveness?

By returning daily to the cross. Forgiveness is rarely instant; it is an ongoing surrender. During fasting, unresolved wounds often surface—not to condemn us, but to heal us. Humility grows as we choose grace again and again.
prayers: Lord, I release those who hurt me. Restore humility through forgiveness. I bring before You every wound, bitterness, and unresolved pain. As You have forgiven me in Christ, I choose to forgive others. Heal my heart and restore humility through grace. Set me free from resentment.

In Matthew 6:14-15, Jesus teaches that God's forgiveness of our sins is conditional upon our forgiveness of others who have wronged us. Pray that we would forgive others as it mirrors God's own merciful nature and His forgiveness of humanity's sins.

Though in the last two years (2024-2025) Malaysia has been able to maintain a low unemployment rate, the same cannot be expected for 2026 when every country will implement their protectionist position. Pray for wisdom for our leaders.

articles.title: Forgetting the Cross
articles.subtitle: Day 30: Saturday, 5 September 2026
articles.content:
Read Philippians 2:5–8; 1 Corinthians 1:18

The greatest threat to humility is forgetting the cross. Philippians 2 reveals Jesus—fully God—choosing obedience, surrender, and self-emptying love. The cross dismantles pride by declaring that salvation is received, not achieved.

When the cross fades from our view, performance rises. When grace fades, pride returns.

How do we overcome this forgetfulness?

By intentionally fixing our eyes on Jesus. Humility is cultivated, not accidental. A cruciform life is shaped daily by surrender, obedience, and love. Fasting restores the cross as our central reference point, reminding us who we are and how we are called to live.
prayers: Jesus, shape my life by Your cross. Lord Jesus, I fix my eyes again on Your cross. Remind me that I am saved by grace, not achievement. Shape my life by Your humility, obedience, and love. Let the way of the cross form the way I live.

The Lord expects us to give our best in service to Him and guard against achieving success that can lead to self-reliance and the neglect of His grace. When we turn our eyes upon Jesus, we see the Son of God who gave His life for us, and our measureless debt erased. Do not forget the cross!

The failed separation of power between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance in the previous Government opened the door of poor accountability in the 1 Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) fund. May we learn from this very expensive lesson as we can ill-afford similar mistakes in the future.
